claim: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) is the methyl donor for nearly all cellular methylation events.
source: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) is the methyl donor for nearly all cellular methylation events.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about SAM's role in cellular methylation.

claim: Cells regulate intracellular SAM levels through intron detention of MAT2A.
source: Cells regulate intracellular SAM levels through intron detention of MAT2A, the only SAM synthetase expressed in most cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by experimental data throughout the paper.

claim: MAT2A is the only SAM synthetase expressed in most cells.
source: Cells regulate intracellular SAM levels through intron detention of MAT2A, the only SAM synthetase expressed in most cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Murray et al., 2019 in the Introduction.

claim: METTL16 promotes splicing of the MAT2A detained intron.
source: The N6-adenosine methyltransferase METTL16 promotes splicing of the MAT2A detained intron by an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript and prior work cited (Pendleton et al., 2017).

claim: The mechanism by which METTL16 promotes MAT2A splicing was unknown prior to this study.
source: The N6-adenosine methyltransferase METTL16 promotes splicing of the MAT2A detained intron by an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: CFIm25 (NUDT21) was identified as a regulator of MAT2A intron detention through a CRISPR knock-out screen.
source: Using an unbiased CRISPR knock-out screen, we identified CFIm25 (NUDT21) as a regulator of MAT2A intron detention and intracellular SAM levels.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: CFIm25 regulates intracellular SAM levels.
source: Using an unbiased CRISPR knock-out screen, we identified CFIm25 (NUDT21) as a regulator of MAT2A intron detention and intracellular SAM levels.
evidence: This is supported by SAM measurement data shown in Figure 2I and Figure 3C.

claim: CFIm25 is a component of the cleavage factor Im (CFIm) complex that regulates poly(A) site selection.
source: CFIm25 is a component of the cleavage factor Im (CFIm) complex that regulates poly(A) site selection, but we show it promotes MAT2A splicing independent of poly(A) site selection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFIm25's known function.

claim: CFIm25 promotes MAT2A splicing independent of poly(A) site selection.
source: CFIm25 is a component of the cleavage factor Im (CFIm) complex that regulates poly(A) site selection, but we show it promotes MAT2A splicing independent of poly(A) site selection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3 showing that APA patterns are similar between HCT116 and 116-ΔDI cells despite different SAM levels.

claim: CFIm25-mediated MAT2A splicing induction requires the RS domains of CFIm68 and CFIm59.
source: CFIm25-mediated MAT2A splicing induction requires the RS domains of its binding partners, CFIm68 and CFIm59 as well as binding sites in the detained intron and 3´ UTR.
evidence: This is supported by tethering assay data in Figure 6E showing that RS domain deletions abolish splicing induction.

claim: CFIm25-mediated MAT2A splicing requires binding sites in the detained intron and 3´ UTR.
source: CFIm25-mediated MAT2A splicing induction requires the RS domains of its binding partners, CFIm68 and CFIm59 as well as binding sites in the detained intron and 3´ UTR.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data in Figure 4 showing that mutations in these sites reduce splicing.

claim: Humans express a single SAM synthetase, encoded by MAT2A, in nearly every tissue except the liver.
source: Humans express a single SAM synthetase, encoded by the gene MAT2A, in nearly every tissue except the liver (Murray et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Murray et al., 2019.

claim: The protein encoded by MAT2A, MATα2, uses ATP and L-methionine to produce SAM.
source: The protein encoded by MAT2A, MATα2, uses ATP and L-methionine to produce SAM.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about MAT2A function.

claim: SAM converts to S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) upon donating a methyl group.
source: Upon donating a methyl group, SAM converts to S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH), which inhibits some methyltransferases (Ferreira de Freitas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SAH inhibits some methyltransferases.
source: Upon donating a methyl group, SAM converts to S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH), which inhibits some methyltransferases (Ferreira de Freitas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ferreira de Freitas et al., 2019.

claim: SAM must be constantly produced to maintain SAM-to-SAH ratios sufficient to support methyltransferase activity.
source: Therefore, SAM must be constantly produced to maintain SAM-to-SAH ratios sufficient to support methyltransferase activity (Clarke, 2006; Krijt et al., 2009; Walsh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Too much or too little methylation of substrates by SAM has been associated with cancer, diabetes, and other diseases.
source: Too much or too little methylation of substrates by SAM has been associated with cancer, diabetes, along with other diseases (Gharipour et al., 2020; McMahon et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Intracellular SAM levels are tightly controlled to maintain homeostasis.
source: Therefore, intracellular SAM levels are tightly controlled to maintain homeostasis, with loss of regulation resulting in cellular dysfunction (Gao et al., 2019; Lio and Huang, 2020; Ouyang et al., 2020; Parkhitko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Loss of SAM regulation results in cellular dysfunction.
source: Therefore, intracellular SAM levels are tightly controlled to maintain homeostasis, with loss of regulation resulting in cellular dysfunction (Gao et al., 2019; Lio and Huang, 2020; Ouyang et al., 2020; Parkhitko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: METTL16 is an N6-methyladenosyl (m6A) transferase.
source: We identified the N6-methyladenosyl (m6A) transferase METTL16 as a key regulator of SAM-responsive MAT2A RNA splicing and proposed that it serves as a critical intracellular SAM sensor (Pendleton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: METTL16 is a key regulator of SAM-responsive MAT2A RNA splicing.
source: We identified the N6-methyladenosyl (m6A) transferase METTL16 as a key regulator of SAM-responsive MAT2A RNA splicing and proposed that it serves as a critical intracellular SAM sensor (Pendleton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited (Pendleton et al., 2017) and data in this manuscript.

claim: METTL16 serves as a critical intracellular SAM sensor.
source: We identified the N6-methyladenosyl (m6A) transferase METTL16 as a key regulator of SAM-responsive MAT2A RNA splicing and proposed that it serves as a critical intracellular SAM sensor (Pendleton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by prior work and data in this manuscript.

claim: METTL16 methylates MAT2A on six evolutionarily conserved hairpins (hp1-hp6) in the 3´ UTR.
source: METTL16 methylates MAT2A on six evolutionarily conserved hairpins (hp1-hp6) in the 3´ untranslated region (3´UTR; Figure 1A; Parker et al., 2011; Pendleton et al., 2017; Warda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MAT2A hairpins contain UACAGARAA motifs which allow for methylation by METTL16 at the A4 position.
source: These hairpins contain UACAGARAA motifs which, in combination with their structure, allows for methylation by METTL16 at the A4 position (underlined)(Doxtader et al., 2018; Mendel et al., 2018; Pendleton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: METTL16 interactions with MAT2A hairpins regulate MAT2A by two mechanisms: mRNA stability and pre-mRNA splicing.
source: METTL16 interactions with MAT2A hairpins regulate MAT2A by two mechanisms, mRNA stability and pre-mRNA splicing.
evidence: This is supported by data in this manuscript and prior citations.

claim: Upon methylation of hp2-6, the stability of the MAT2A mRNA decreases.
source: Upon methylation of hp2-6, the stability of the MAT2A mRNA decreases (Martínez-Chantar et al., 2003; Pendleton et al., 2017; Shima et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In SAM-limiting conditions, reduced methylation of hp2-6 stabilizes the MAT2A mRNA.
source: In SAM-limiting conditions, reduced methylation of hp2-6 stabilizes the MAT2A mRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous statement and supported by the cited literature.

claim: The hp2-6 mechanism likely reflects the typical 'reader-writer' paradigm in which m6A marks are read by m6A-specific binding proteins.
source: This mechanism likely reflects the typical 'reader-writer' paradigm in which m6A marks are read by m6A-specific binding proteins (Meyer and Jaffrey, 2017; Yue et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to general m6A biology.

claim: In SAM-rich conditions, METTL16 methylates hp1 then dissociates, resulting in increased retention of the last intron.
source: Our working model proposes that in SAM-rich conditions, METTL16 methylates hp1 then dissociates, resulting in increased retention of the last intron (Figure 1A; Pendleton et al., 2017; Pendleton et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by prior work and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Failure to excise the last intron of MAT2A results in nuclear retention and degradation of the transcript.
source: Failure to excise the last intron of MAT2A results in nuclear retention and degradation of the transcript, defining this intron as a detained intron (DI)(Boutz et al., 2015; Bresson et al., 2015; Pendleton et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The last intron of MAT2A is a detained intron (DI).
source: Failure to excise the last intron of MAT2A results in nuclear retention and degradation of the transcript, defining this intron as a detained intron (DI)(Boutz et al., 2015; Bresson et al., 2015; Pendleton et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data throughout the manuscript.

claim: During SAM starvation, METTL16 binds hp1 but low SAM levels lead to decreased enzymatic turnover of METTL16.
source: During SAM starvation, METTL16 binds hp1 but low SAM levels lead to decreased enzymatic turnover of METTL16.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model supported by prior work.

claim: Increased METTL16 occupancy on hp1 promotes splicing of the final MAT2A intron.
source: The resulting increased METTL16 occupancy on hp1 promotes splicing of the final MAT2A intron.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model supported by data in this manuscript and prior work.

claim: Two carboxyl-terminal vertebrate conserved regions (VCR) in METTL16 are necessary and sufficient to promote splicing of MAT2A reporters.
source: Two carboxyl-terminal vertebrate conserved regions (VCR) in METTL16 are necessary and sufficient to promote splicing of MAT2A reporters and increase the affinity of METTL16 for RNA (Aoyama et al., 2020; Pendleton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The VCR domains of METTL16 increase the affinity of METTL16 for RNA.
source: Two carboxyl-terminal vertebrate conserved regions (VCR) in METTL16 are necessary and sufficient to promote splicing of MAT2A reporters and increase the affinity of METTL16 for RNA (Aoyama et al., 2020; Pendleton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: METTL16 functions as both the m6A reader and writer with respect to hp1 and regulation of intron detention.
source: Thus, with respect to hp1 and regulation of intron detention, METTL16 functions as both the m6A reader and writer.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data and model presented.

claim: METTL16 lacks recognizable splicing domains.
source: However, METTL16 lacks recognizable splicing domains and has no known protein interacting partners, so its mechanism for promoting splicing of the MAT2A DI has been unclear (Ignatova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: METTL16 has no known protein interacting partners.
source: However, METTL16 lacks recognizable splicing domains and has no known protein interacting partners, so its mechanism for promoting splicing of the MAT2A DI has been unclear (Ignatova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation and the authors' own unpublished data mentioned in the Discussion.

claim: Splicing of terminal introns is coupled with 3´-end formation.
source: Splicing of terminal introns is coupled with 3´-end formation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Definition of both the 5´ and 3´ ends of an exon is necessary for efficient splicing.
source: Definition of both the 5´ and 3´ ends of an exon is necessary for efficient splicing, but terminal exons lack 3´ definition as there are no downstream introns (De Conti et al., 2013; Martinson, 2011; Niwa et al., 1992; Niwa et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Terminal exons lack 3´ definition as there are no downstream introns.
source: Definition of both the 5´ and 3´ ends of an exon is necessary for efficient splicing, but terminal exons lack 3´ definition as there are no downstream introns (De Conti et al., 2013; Martinson, 2011; Niwa et al., 1992; Niwa et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Splicing factors and 3´ end formation machinery directly interact during the definition of the terminal exon.
source: Instead, splicing factors and 3´ end formation machinery directly interact during the definition of the terminal exon (Davidson and West, 2013; Dettwiler et al., 2004; Kyburz et al., 2006; Lutz et al., 1996; McCracken et al., 2002; Millevoi et al., 2006; Rappsilber et al., 2002; Shi et al., 2009; Vagner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Splicing of terminal exons and 3´ end formation enhance each other.
source: While splicing of terminal exons and 3´ end formation enhance each other, the mechanisms of this coupling remain incompletely understood.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The mechanisms of coupling between terminal exon splicing and 3´ end formation remain incompletely understood.
source: While splicing of terminal exons and 3´ end formation enhance each other, the mechanisms of this coupling remain incompletely understood.
evidence: This establishes a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The CFIm complex is a component of the 3´-end formation machinery.
source: The cleavage factor Im complex (CFIm) is a component of the 3´-end formation machinery with characteristics that suggest it links 3´ end formation with splicing (Hardy and Norbury, 2016; Martinson, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CFIm complex has characteristics that suggest it links 3´ end formation with splicing.
source: The cleavage factor Im complex (CFIm) is a component of the 3´-end formation machinery with characteristics that suggest it links 3´ end formation with splicing (Hardy and Norbury, 2016; Martinson, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on known characteristics of CFIm and supported by citations.

claim: The CFIm complex consists of a dimer of CFIm25 and each CFIm25 interacts with a monomer of CFIm68 or CFIm59 to form a heterotetrameric CFIm complex.
source: The CFIm complex consists of a dimer of CFIm25 (NUDT21, CPSF5) and each CFIm25 interacts with a monomer of CFIm68 (CPSF6) or CFIm59 (CPSF7) to form a heterotetrameric CFIm complex (Kim et al., 2010; Rüegsegger et al., 1996; Rüegsegger et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFIm complex composition supported by citations.

claim: The CFIm complex was identified as a 3´-end formation factor.
source: The CFIm complex was identified as a 3´-end formation factor, but more recent work suggests it is not required for polyadenylation of all mRNAs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: CFIm is not required for polyadenylation of all mRNAs.
source: The CFIm complex was identified as a 3´-end formation factor, but more recent work suggests it is not required for polyadenylation of all mRNAs.
evidence: This is based on more recent work in the field.

claim: CFIm is an enhancer that regulates the efficiency of poly(A) site usage.
source: Instead, CFIm is an enhancer that regulates the efficiency of poly(A) site usage (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Knockdown of CFIm components leads to widespread changes in polyadenylation, with the predominant effect being a shift to proximal poly(A) site usage.
source: As a result, knockdown of CFIm components leads to widespread changes in polyadenylation, with the predominant effect being a shift to proximal poly(A) site usage (Brumbaugh et al., 2018; Gruber et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2012; Masamha et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: CFIm68 and CFIm59 contain arginine- and serine-rich regions (RS domains) that aid in 3´ end formation.
source: CFIm68 and CFIm59 contain arginine- and serine-rich regions (RS domains) that aid in 3´ end formation (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: RS domains are common components of splicing factors.
source: However, RS domains are common components of splicing factors, suggesting a role for CFIm68 and CFIm59 in splicing (Dettwiler et al., 2004; Hardy and Norbury, 2016; Long and Caceres, 2009; Millevoi et al., 2006; Rappsilber et al., 2002; Rüegsegger et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The presence of RS domains in CFIm68 and CFIm59 suggests a role for these proteins in splicing.
source: However, RS domains are common components of splicing factors, suggesting a role for CFIm68 and CFIm59 in splicing (Dettwiler et al., 2004; Hardy and Norbury, 2016; Long and Caceres, 2009; Millevoi et al., 2006; Rappsilber et al., 2002; Rüegsegger et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of RS domains.

claim: There has been little direct evidence that any specific pre-mRNA requires CFIm as a splicing factor independent of its functions in poly(A) site selection.
source: To date, there has been little direct evidence that any specific pre-mRNA requires CFIm as a splicing factor independent of its functions in poly(A) site selection.
evidence: This establishes a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Knockdown of METTL16 abrogates the cell's ability to induce production of the endogenous MAT2A or reporter mRNA after methionine depletion.
source: Similarly, knockdown of METTL16 abrogates the cell's ability to induce production of the endogenous MAT2A or reporter mRNA after methionine depletion (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The production of the reporter mRNA reflects that of the endogenous MAT2A.
source: Together, these observations demonstrate that the production of our reporter mRNA reflects that of the endogenous MAT2A.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The reporter mRNA from the clonal line unexpectedly splices the β-globin 5´ splice site to the MAT2A 3´ splice acceptor.
source: Despite its usefulness in our studies (see below), we found that the reporter mRNA from our clonal line unexpectedly splices the β-globin 5´ splice site to the MAT2A 3´ splice acceptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: The alternative splicing of the reporter line results in a more stable protein product.
source: Thus, the alternative splicing of the reporter line results in a more stable protein product and therefore more useful reporter.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: METTL16 was the top candidate in the CRISPR screen.
source: The top candidate was METTL16 which supports the efficacy of the screen.
evidence: This is supported by the CRISPR screen data in Figure 1G.

claim: MED9 and NUDT21 (CFIm25) were hits in the CRISPR screen after exclusion of genes on chromosome 19.
source: After exclusion of genes on chromosome 19, three hits remained. The top candidate was METTL16 which supports the efficacy of the screen. The other hits were MED9 and NUDT21 (CPSF5).
evidence: This is supported by the CRISPR screen data in Figure 1G and Supplementary file 1.

claim: MED9 is a member of the mediator complex, a coactivator of RNA pol II.
source: MED9 is a member of the mediator complex, a coactivator of RNA pol II (Soutourina, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CFIm25 is associated with RS domain-containing proteins CFIm68 and CFIm59.
source: Given its association with RS domain-containing proteins CFIm68 and CFIm59, we decided to investigate potential functions for CFIm25 in the regulated splicing of MAT2A.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFIm complex composition.

claim: CFIm25 depletion results in lower mRNA accumulation of the reporter.
source: Similar to METTL16 knockdown, we observed that CFIm25 depletion resulted in lower mRNA accumulation (Figure 2A–C and E, 'Reporter') and a modest increase in the DI isoform (Figure 2B and D–E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, 'Reporter').
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: CFIm25 depletion results in a modest increase in the DI isoform of the reporter.
source: Similar to METTL16 knockdown, we observed that CFIm25 depletion resulted in lower mRNA accumulation (Figure 2A–C and E, 'Reporter') and a modest increase in the DI isoform (Figure 2B and D–E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, 'Reporter').
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mutation of hp2-6 eliminates METTL16-dependent contributions to cytoplasmic stability of the mRNA isoform.
source: More importantly, we mutated hp2-6 thereby eliminating METTL16-dependent contributions to cytoplasmic stability of the mRNA isoform (Figure 2A, bottom).
evidence: This is based on prior work showing hp2-6 regulates mRNA stability.

claim: CFIm25 knockdown decreases mRNA accumulation and increases intron detention in the hp2-6 mutant reporter.
source: Using two independent clonal cell lines ('T2A, hp2-6m9#1' and 'T2A, hp2-6m9#2'), we observed decreases in mRNA accumulation and increases in intron detention in this reporter after METTL16 or CFIm25 depletion (Figure 2B–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The hp2-6-independent effects of CFIm25 knockdown on reporter mRNA and DI isoform levels are consistent with a role for CFIm25 in the induction of MAT2A splicing.
source: These hp2-6-independent effects of CFIm25 knockdown on reporter mRNA and DI isoform levels are consistent with a role for CFIm25 in the induction of MAT2A splicing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 2.

claim: CFIm25 depletion increases intron detention of endogenous MAT2A under methionine-free conditions.
source: CFIm25 depletion using two independent siRNAs increased intron detention under methionine-free conditions, phenocopying METTL16 depletion (Figure 2F, red).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CFIm25 depletion increases intron detention of endogenous MAT2A in methionine-replete media.
source: Interestingly, there was also a slight but significant increase in intron detention in methionine-replete media (Figure 2F, blue), further supporting a role for CFIm25 in the regulation of MAT2A intron detention.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CFIm25 knockdown does not affect METTL16 expression.
source: CFIm25 knockdown did not affect METTL16 expression (Figure 2G), so CFIm25 does not regulate MAT2A expression by manipulation of METTL16 abundance.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: CFIm25 does not regulate MAT2A expression by manipulation of METTL16 abundance.
source: CFIm25 knockdown did not affect METTL16 expression (Figure 2G), so CFIm25 does not regulate MAT2A expression by manipulation of METTL16 abundance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 2G.

claim: Co-depletion of METTL16 and CFIm25 has no greater effects on MAT2A RNA than depletion of each individual factor.
source: Indeed, co-depletion had no greater effects on MAT2A RNA than depletion of each individual factor (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Depletion of CFIm25 decreases intracellular SAM levels under methionine-rich conditions.
source: Finally, we assessed SAM levels in cells depleted of CFIm25 and found that, like METTL16, depletion of CFIm25 decreased intracellular SAM levels under methionine-rich conditions (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: CFIm25 is necessary for production of SAM by regulating MAT2A splicing.
source: Together, these data support the hypothesis that that CFIm25 is necessary for production of SAM by regulating MAT2A splicing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Knockdown of CFIm25 results in global changes in poly(A) site usage.
source: Knockdown of CFIm25 results in global changes in poly(A) site usage.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations earlier in the manuscript.

claim: A minor isoform of MAT2A using a weak, proximal poly(A) site in the 3´UTR has previously been detected.
source: Indeed, a minor isoform of MAT2A using a weak, proximal poly(A) site in the 3´UTR has previously been detected (Routh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The proximal MAT2A poly(A) isoform is not responsive to methionine levels nor depletion of METTL16 or CFIm25 in 293A-TOA cells.
source: Importantly, neither was responsive to methionine levels nor depletion of METTL16 or CFIm25 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The observed changes in MAT2A expression and SAM levels in 293A-TOA cells are not due to CFIm-mediated changes in MAT2A poly(A) site usage.
source: APA patterns can be cell-type specific (see below), but these data support the conclusion that the observed changes in MAT2A expression and SAM levels in 293A-TOA cells (Figure 2F and I) are not due to CFIm-mediated changes in MAT2A poly(A) site usage.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The 116-ΔDI cell line is heterozygotic with one allele containing the precisely deleted DI from homologous repair and the second allele deleting the DI via non-homologous end joining.
source: Although we used a donor plasmid to promote homologous repair (HR) upon cleavage of two sites flanking the DI (Figure 3A), the resulting clonal line (116-ΔDI) is heterozygotic. One allele contains the expected precisely deleted DI from HR while the second allele deletes the DI via non-homologous end joining (NHEJ).
evidence: This is supported by the description in the text and Figure 3A.

claim: No MAT2A-DI isoform was detected by northern blot in 116-ΔDI cells.
source: As expected, no MAT2A-DI isoform was detected by northern blot, but methionine depletion leads to an increase of MAT2A mRNA, presumably due to hp2-6-mediated stabilization of the mRNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Methionine depletion leads to an increase of MAT2A mRNA in 116-ΔDI cells, presumably due to hp2-6-mediated stabilization.
source: As expected, no MAT2A-DI isoform was detected by northern blot, but methionine depletion leads to an increase of MAT2A mRNA, presumably due to hp2-6-mediated stabilization of the mRNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and is an inference based on known hp2-6 function.

claim: CFIm25 depletion has no effect on the methionine responsiveness of MAT2A mRNA in 116-ΔDI cells.
source: Additionally, CFIm25 depletion had no effect on the methionine responsiveness of MAT2A mRNA in 116-ΔDI cells, consistent with a function for CFIm25 in regulation of the MAT2A DI (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SAM levels decrease upon METTL16 or CFIm25 depletion in HCT116 cells.
source: Similar to 293A-TOA cells (Figure 2I), SAM levels decreased upon METTL16 or CFIm25 depletion in HCT116 cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: METTL16 or CFIm25 depletion does not decrease SAM levels in 116-ΔDI cells.
source: In marked contrast, these treatments did not decrease SAM levels in 116-ΔDI cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CFIm25 regulates SAM by regulation of the MAT2A DI.
source: This observation strongly supports the conclusion that CFIm25 regulates SAM by regulation of the MAT2A DI.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 3C.

claim: Over 2500 poly(A) site changes were detected due to CFIm25 depletion by PAC-seq.
source: We detected over 2500 poly(A) site changes due to CFIm25 depletion (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by PAC-seq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The overwhelming majority of poly(A) site changes upon CFIm25 depletion were reductions in the percent distal usage (PDU).
source: Consistent with previous reports that depletion of CFIm25 favors the use of proximal poly(A) sites, the overwhelming majority of changes were reductions in the percent distal usage (PDU) of poly(A) sites (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Nearly identical levels of poly(A) site shortening were observed in 116-ΔDI compared to HCT116 upon CFIm25 depletion.
source: Importantly, nearly identical levels of shortening were observed in 116-ΔDI (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Only 45 and 20 genes experienced APA when comparing HCT116 and 116-ΔDI lines under siNT and siCFIm25 conditions, respectively.
source: In fact, when we compared the parental and 116-ΔDI lines under either knockdown condition, only 45 and 20 genes experienced APA for the siNT and siCFIm25, respectively (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F–G.

claim: Many exons with significant changes in APA were consistent between HCT116 and 116-ΔDI.
source: Additionally, many exons with significant changes in APA were consistent between HCT116 and 116-ΔDI (Figure 3H–J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3H–J.

claim: CFIm25's role in SAM regulation and APA are separable.
source: Because the APA patterns were largely similar even though the SAM levels differ upon CFIm25 knockdown (Figure 3C), these global analyses support our conclusion that CFIm25's role in SAM regulation and APA are separable.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 3.

claim: CFIm25 regulates MAT2A mRNA abundance in a MAT2A DI-dependent fashion.
source: They also strengthen the conclusion that CFIm25 regulates MAT2A mRNA abundance in a MAT2A DI-dependent fashion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 3.

claim: All three components of the CFIm complex cross-linked to varying degrees to the 11 UGUA motifs downstream of hp1 in the MAT2A 3´UTR.
source: All three components of the CFIm complex cross-linked to varying degrees to the 11 UGUA motifs downstream of hp1 in the MAT2A 3´UTR (Figure 4A, ds-UGUA, blue hexagons).
evidence: This is based on publicly available CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutation of the last UGUA motif in the 3´UTR had no effect on MAT2A intron detention.
source: Because this mutation had no effect on intron detention (Figure 4C–D, dark blue), we then mutated ten out of eleven sites found in the 3´UTR to CGUA, UCUA, or UGCA (Figure 4C, 10/11).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C–D.

claim: The 10/11 UGUA mutant construct had similar splicing efficiency as wild type.
source: The 10/11 construct had similar splicing efficiency as wild type, suggesting the downstream UGUA motifs are not involved in MAT2A splicing (Figure 4C–D, light blue).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C–D.

claim: The downstream UGUA motifs in the 3´UTR are not involved in MAT2A splicing.
source: The 10/11 construct had similar splicing efficiency as wild type, suggesting the downstream UGUA motifs are not involved in MAT2A splicing (Figure 4C–D, light blue).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 4C–D.

claim: An evolutionarily conserved UGUA motif is found in the MAT2A DI 9–12 nt upstream of the 3´ splice site.
source: An evolutionarily conserved UGUA motif is found in the DI 9–12 nt upstream of the 3´ splice site, overlapping with a CFIm complex CLIP-seq peak (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and CLIP-seq data in Figure 4A.

claim: Two independent point mutations in the DI UGUA motif significantly abrogated MAT2A splicing.
source: We found that both mutations significantly abrogated MAT2A splicing both at basal levels and upon methionine depletion (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E–F.

claim: Intronic assembly of the CFIm complex may contribute to MAT2A splicing.
source: Thus, intronic assembly of the CFIm complex may contribute to MAT2A splicing.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the data in Figure 4E–F.

claim: The strongest and most consistent CLIP-seq peak among all three CFIm factors lies immediately upstream of hp1 and downstream of the stop codon.
source: The strongest and most consistent CLIP-seq peak among all three CFIm factors lies immediately upstream of hp1 and downstream of the stop codon (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The CLIP-seq peak upstream of hp1 centers on a UGUU motif that is evolutionarily conserved in vertebrates.
source: There is no UGUA element, but the peak centers on a UGUU motif that is evolutionarily conserved in vertebrates, except in Danio rerio where it is a UGUA, the canonical CFIm25 binding site (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mutation of the UGUU to UGCU decreased MAT2A splicing efficiency.
source: We mutated the UGUU to UGCU which decreased splicing efficiency comparably to that of the DI point mutations (Figure 4G–H, dark red).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4G–H.

claim: Replacing the UGUU with UGUA did not change splicing efficiency.
source: We observed no changes in splicing efficiency when the UGUU motif was replaced with the canonical UGUA sequence (Figure 4G–H, pink).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4G–H.

claim: Depletion of METTL16 or CFIm25 resulted in reduced ability to induce splicing of the wild-type UGUU and UGUA constructs.
source: Additionally, depletion of METTL16 or CFIm25 resulted in reduced ability to induce splicing of the wild-type UGUU and UGUA constructs, while no change was observed for the UGCU mutation to abrogate splicing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The non-consensus UGUU binding site contributes to the splicing of the MAT2A DI.
source: Thus, this non-consensus binding site for CFIm appears to contribute to the splicing of the MAT2A DI.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 4G–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CFIm25 crosslinked the substrates containing either the canonical UGUA or UGUU motifs more efficiently than to the UGCU substrate.
source: We found that CFIm25 crosslinked the substrates containing either the canonical UGUA or UGUU motifs more efficiently than to the UGCU substrate (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by label transfer assay data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Cold UGCU RNA was a significantly less efficient competitor than UGUU or UGUA RNAs in competition assays.
source: Cold UGCU RNA was a significantly less efficient competitor than UGUU or UGUA RNAs (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: CFIm25 binds the UGUU motif in MAT2A's 3´UTR to regulate intron detention.
source: Together, the CLIP-seq (Martin et al., 2012), reporter assays, and in vitro binding all suggest that CFIm25 binds to a noncanonical UGUU motif in MAT2A's 3´UTR to regulate intron detention.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including CLIP-seq, reporter assays, and in vitro binding data.

claim: Depletion of CFIm59 with two different siRNAs individually or in combination had no significant effects on MAT2A intron detention.
source: Depletion of CFIm59 with two different siRNAs individually or in combination had no significant effects on MAT2A intron detention, while depletion of CFIm68 had modest effect for only one siRNA (Figure 5A–B; #1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: Depletion of CFIm68 had modest effect on MAT2A intron detention for only one siRNA.
source: Depletion of CFIm59 with two different siRNAs individually or in combination had no significant effects on MAT2A intron detention, while depletion of CFIm68 had modest effect for only one siRNA (Figure 5A–B; #1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: Co-depletion of CFIm68 and CFIm59 increased intron detention upon methionine depletion.
source: In contrast, co-depletion of CFIm68 and CFIm59 increased intron detention upon methionine depletion, with a significant increase in intron detention relative to CFIm68 knockdown alone (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: MAT2A intron detention is nearly identical after exposing cells to media with different methionine concentrations upon CFIm68 and CFIm59 co-depletion, METTL16, or CFIm25 depletion.
source: In addition, MAT2A intron detention is nearly identical after exposing cells to media with different methionine concentrations upon CFIm68 and CFIm59 co-depletion, METTL16, or CFIm25 depletion (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: There is possible functional redundancy between CFIm68 and CFIm59 in the splicing of MAT2A.
source: These results suggest possible functional redundancy between CFIm68 and CFIm59 in the splicing of MAT2A, consistent with the lack of identification of either gene in our CRISPR screen (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the data in Figure 5.

claim: Tethering wild-type CFIm25 induced splicing to levels comparable with METTL16 tethering.
source: First, we tethered wild-type (wt) CFIm25 under methionine-rich conditions and observed splicing induction to levels comparable with METTL16 tethering (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: CFIm25 mutants that bind neither CFIm68 nor CFIm59 showed a significant loss in splicing induction when tethered.
source: Upon tethering of these CFIm mutants, we observed a significant loss in splicing induction suggesting that a functional CFIm complex is responsible for splicing (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A functional CFIm complex is responsible for MAT2A splicing.
source: Upon tethering of these CFIm mutants, we observed a significant loss in splicing induction suggesting that a functional CFIm complex is responsible for splicing (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 6B.

claim: Tethering of an RNA-binding mutant (m3, R63S) of CFIm25 maintained splicing activity.
source: In contrast, tethering of an RNA-binding mutant (m3, R63S) of CFIm25 maintained splicing activity, as expected since RNA binding is driven by MS2 tethering (Yang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and is consistent with the tethering mechanism.

claim: CFIm68 and CFIm59 tethering was sufficient to induce splicing.
source: As predicted, CFIm68 and CFIm59 tethering was sufficient to induce splicing, while the ΔRS proteins were unable to affect intron detention (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: CFIm68 and CFIm59 lacking the RS domains were unable to affect intron detention when tethered.
source: As predicted, CFIm68 and CFIm59 tethering was sufficient to induce splicing, while the ΔRS proteins were unable to affect intron detention (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The CFIm complex is responsible for the splicing of the MAT2A DI.
source: Together, these observations suggest that the CFIm complex is responsible for the splicing of the MAT2A DI.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the tethering data in Figure 6.

claim: CFIm is downstream of METTL16 in the MAT2A splicing induction mechanism.
source: Our data suggest the model for CFIm complex-mediated induction of MAT2A splicing shown in Figure 7A. CFIm is recruited to the UGUA in the DI and UGUU in MAT2A 3´UTR. Upon CFIm binding, CFIm68 and CFIm59 serve as the downstream effectors that promote efficient splicing of the DI through their RS domains. This model predicts that CFIm is downstream of the SAM sensor METTL16.
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Tethering of METTL16 fails to induce splicing after CFIm25 depletion.
source: Indeed, the tethering of METTL16 fails to induce splicing after CFIm25 depletion compared to the non-target and no MS2 controls (Figure 7B, gray and orange).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Tethering of CFIm25 after METTL16 depletion results in splicing induction comparable to the non-targeting control.
source: As expected, tethering of CFIm25 after METTL16 depletion results in splicing induction comparable to the non-targeting control (Figure 7B, gray and purple).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: METTL16 acts as the upstream SAM sensor while CFIm directly mediates the splicing of MAT2A.
source: This supports the idea that METTL16 acts as the upstream SAM sensor while CFIm directly mediates the splicing of MAT2A.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 7B.

claim: CFIm68/CFIm59 co-depletion reduces splicing induction upon METTL16 or CFIm25 tethering.
source: Consistent with this prediction, CFIm68/CFIm59 co-depletion reduces splicing induction upon METTL16 or CFIm25 tethering (Figure 7C, green).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Depletion of CFIm68 alone had similar effects as CFIm68/CFIm59 co-depletion on tethering-induced splicing.
source: Surprisingly, depletion of CFIm68 alone had similar effects as CFIm68/CFIm59 co-depletion, while CFIm59 depletion was comparable to the non-targeting control.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Tethering CFIm68 induces splicing in CFIm25-depleted cells.
source: We likewise observed that tethering CFIm68 induces splicing in CFIm25-depleted cells, but CFIm59 did not (Figure 7D, orange).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Tethering CFIm68 is sufficient to induce splicing of MAT2A in the absence of METTL16 or other CFIm complex family members.
source: These data demonstrate that tethering CFIm68 is sufficient to induce splicing of MAT2A in the absence of METTL16 or other CFIm complex family members.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 7D.

claim: The function of CFIm59 in MAT2A splicing is less clear but it may contribute to splicing redundantly with CFIm68 or have other functions.
source: The function of CFIm59 in MAT2A splicing is less clear, but it may contribute to splicing redundantly with CFIm68 or have other functions in MAT2A splicing or CFIm complex assembly (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the data.

claim: MAT2A splicing regulation is independent of CFIm's role in 3´ end formation.
source: Our data suggest that MAT2A splicing regulation is independent of its role in 3´ end formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 3.

claim: CFIm25 has recently been reported to affect regulation of the glutaminase (GLS) gene in a complex regulatory paradigm that includes alternative splicing and APA.
source: However, CFIm25 has recently been reported to affect regulation of the glutaminase (GLS) gene in a complex regulatory paradigm that includes alternative splicing and APA (Masamha et al., 2014; Redis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: CFIm25 promotes the accumulation of the GAC isoform of GLS.
source: CFIm25 promotes the accumulation of the GAC isoform, suggesting it defines this alternative last exon by promoting usage of its poly(A) site and/or the 3´ splice site.
evidence: This is based on cited work on GLS regulation.

claim: The 3´ splice site of the GAC isoform has a weak polypyrimidine tract and includes a UGUA within 20 nt of the 3´ AG splice site, similar to MAT2A.
source: Interestingly, the 3´ splice site of the GAC isoform has a weak polypyrimidine tract and includes a UGUA within 20 nt of the 3´ AG splice site, similar to MAT2A.
evidence: This is an observation based on sequence analysis.

claim: Other genes may require CFIm binding near a 3´ splice site to promote splicing.
source: Thus, other genes may require CFIm binding near a 3´ splice site to promote splicing, but the extent of the phenomenon is unclear.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the GLS and MAT2A examples.

claim: The authors were unsuccessful in coimmunoprecipitating METTL16 and CFIm25.
source: The simplest model is that METTL16 recruits CFIm to the RNA, but we were unsuccessful in coimmunoprecipitating METTL16 and CFIm25.
evidence: This is a statement about negative experimental results.

claim: Unpublished yeast two-hybrid experiments and coimmunoprecipitation mass spectrometry experiments were consistent with a published report that found no METTL16-binding proteins.
source: Additionally, our unpublished yeast two-hybrid experiments and coimmunoprecipitation mass spectrometry experiments were consistent with a published report that found no METTL16-binding proteins (Ignatova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by unpublished data and citation.

claim: If METTL16 and CFIm25 directly interact, this interaction is likely transient.
source: It seems unlikely that METTL16 functions without other binding partners, but if METTL16 and CFIm25 directly interact, this interaction is likely transient.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the inability to detect the interaction.

claim: METTL16 may mediate CFIm25 binding to MAT2A through an RNA conformational change that exposes the binding sites.
source: Alternatively, METTL16 may mediate CFIm25 binding to MAT2A through an RNA conformational change that exposes the binding sites.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative model.

claim: The VCR domain of METTL16 binds RNA.
source: This conformational change hypothesis is supported by the discovery that the VCR domain of METTL16 binds RNA (Aoyama et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The VCR domain alone can drive splicing when tethered to a reporter.
source: Since the VCR domains alone can drive splicing when tethered to a reporter (Pendleton et al., 2017), the VCR domain could alter RNA secondary structure surrounding hp1 thereby allowing CFIm25 binding.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Other RNA, proteins, or posttranslational modifications may promote the transient formation of the METTL16:CFIm complex on the MAT2A transcript.
source: Alternatively, other RNA, proteins, or posttranslational modifications may promote the transient formation of the METTL16:CFIm complex on the MAT2A transcript.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative model.

claim: Mutation of either the DI UGUA or 3´UTR UGUU results in abrogation of splicing to comparable levels.
source: Mutation of either the DI UGUA or 3´UTR UGUU results in abrogation of splicing to comparable levels, suggesting that both sites contribute equally to the splicing of MAT2A (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E–H.

claim: Both the DI UGUA and 3´UTR UGUU sites contribute equally to the splicing of MAT2A.
source: Mutation of either the DI UGUA or 3´UTR UGUU results in abrogation of splicing to comparable levels, suggesting that both sites contribute equally to the splicing of MAT2A (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 4E–H.

claim: The two CFIm binding sites could independently function or be bound simultaneously with the intervening RNA looped out.
source: The two sites could independently function as CFIm binding sites. Alternatively, since CFIm25 exists as dimer within the complex, it is possible that the sites are bound simultaneously with the intervening RNA looped out.
evidence: This presents two alternative models.

claim: Previous data suggests looping may be important for the function of CFIm25.
source: In fact, previous data suggests looping may be important for the function of CFIm25 (Yang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Two UGUA motifs in the PAPOLA mRNA 3´UTR simultaneously bind to the CFIm25 dimer to promote more efficient binding.
source: Two UGUA motifs in the PAPOLA mRNA 3´UTR simultaneously bind to the CFIm25 dimer to promote more efficient binding.
evidence: This is based on cited work.

claim: The two UGUA motifs in PAPOLA must be at least nine nt apart to allow for looping.
source: The two sites must be at least nine nt apart to allow for looping, but the upper limit of distance between UGUA motifs has yet to be determined.
evidence: This is based on cited work.

claim: The MAT2A DI UGUA and UGUU motif upstream of hp1 are 114 nt apart allowing ample separation for RNA looping.
source: The MAT2A DI UGUA and UGUU motif upstream of hp1 are 114 nt apart allowing ample separation for RNA looping.
evidence: This is a factual statement based on sequence analysis.

claim: It has been proposed that RNA looping mediated by the CFIm complex regulates poly(A) site selection by occluding or presenting poly(A) sites.
source: It has been proposed that RNA looping mediated by the CFIm complex regulates poly(A) site selection by occluding or presenting poly(A) sites (Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a proposed model from cited work.

claim: CFIm-dependent RNA looping has not been demonstrated in cells.
source: However, to our knowledge, this has yet to be demonstrated in cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The polypyrimidine tract in the MAT2A DI is interrupted by three purines, two of which are part of the UGUA.
source: The polypyrimidine tract in the MAT2A DI is interrupted by three purines, two of which are the part of the UGUA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The same sequence that weakens the polypyrimidine tract also provides a regulatory CFIm binding site capable of overcoming inefficient splicing.
source: Thus, our data suggest that the same sequence that weakens the polypyrimidine tract also provides a regulatory CFIm binding site capable of overcoming inefficient splicing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data and sequence analysis.

claim: U2AF's RRMs are separated by a flexible linker and each interacts with ~4–5 nt.
source: Consistent with this idea, U2AF's RRMs are separated by a flexible linker and each interacts with ~4–5 nt (Agrawal et al., 2016; Jenkins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: As many as ~12% of introns may be U2AF-independent.
source: In fact, as many as ~12% of introns may be U2AF-independent (Shao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: U2AF can be functionally substituted by SPF45/RBM17 on a subset of introns.
source: In addition, U2AF can be functionally substituted by SPF45/RBM17 on a subset of introns (Fukumura et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: In vitro U2AF depletion can be complemented by excess SR proteins.
source: Moreover, in vitro U2AF depletion can be complemented by excess SR proteins (MacMillan et al., 1997), so it is not unreasonable to suggest that the RS domains of CFIm may supply this function for MAT2A DI.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: In knockdown experiments CFIm68 and CFIm59 appear to be redundant for splicing.
source: We have determined that the CFIm complex is necessary for the splicing of MAT2A, but the composition of this complex is unclear. In our knockdown experiments CFIm68 and CFIm59 appear to be redundant for splicing (Figure 5) and neither appeared as CRISPR screen hits (Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 5.

claim: Tethering of either CFIm68 or CFIm59 resulted in comparable splicing induction, as long as an RS domain is present.
source: Further supporting functional redundancy, tethering of either CFIm68 or CFIm59 resulted in comparable splicing induction, as long as an RS domain is present (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: CFIm68 and CFIm59 have non-redundant function in cells.
source: Despite CFIm68 and CFIm59 belonging to the same complex and sharing significant sequence and structural similarity, CFIm68 and CFIm59 have non-redundant function in cells (Deng et al., 2019; Li et al., 2011; Tresaugues et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Knockdown of CFIm68 leads to a global shift to proximal poly(A) site usage, similarly to CFIm25 knockdown, while CFIm59 has no effect.
source: Knockdown of CFIm68 leads to a global shift to proximal poly(A) site usage, similarly to CFIm25 knockdown, while CFIm59 has no effect (Gruber et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: CFIm68 and CFIm59 have distinct interaction partners.
source: Additionally, CFIm68 and CFIm59 have distinct interaction partners (Martin et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2010; Millevoi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: When tethered, CFIm25 is incapable of promoting splicing in the absence of CFIm68.
source: When tethered, CFIm25 is incapable of promoting splicing in the absence of CFIm68, while CFIm59 knockdown alone has no effect (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Tethering of CFIm68 enables splicing independent of CFIm25, while CFIm59 requires CFIm25.
source: Additionally, tethering of CFIm68 enables splicing independent of CFIm25, while CFIm59 requires CFIm25 (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The CFIm complex is a major regulator of poly(A) site selection.
source: The CFIm complex is a major regulator of poly(A) site selection (Brumbaugh et al., 2018; Gruber et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2012; Masamha et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CFIm complex's role in MAT2A splicing and SAM metabolism appear to be independent of poly(A) site selection.
source: Our data show that the CFIm complex's role in MAT2A splicing and SAM metabolism appear to be independent of poly(A) site selection (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 3D–G.

claim: The shortening of 3´UTRs upon CFIm knockdown has been linked to important biological phenotypes including cancer cell proliferation and cell differentiation.
source: The shortening of 3´UTRs upon CFIm knockdown has been linked to important biological phenotypes including cancer cell proliferation and cell differentiation (Brumbaugh et al., 2018; Chu et al., 2019; Jafari Najaf Abadi et al., 2019; Masamha et al., 2014; Tamaddon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Knockdown of either CFIm25 or CFIm68 increases transcription-factor-induced reprogramming of mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC).
source: For example, knockdown of either CFIm25 or CFIm68 increases transcription-factor-induced reprogramming of mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC)(Brumbaugh et al., 2018; Ji and Tian, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The increased reprogramming upon CFIm knockdown is attributed to global shifts from distal poly(A) site usage to proximal, which is characteristic of less differentiated and more proliferative cells.
source: This effect is attributed to global shifts from distal poly(A) site usage to proximal, which is characteristic of less differentiated and more proliferative cells (Ji et al., 2009; Mayr and Bartel, 2009; Sandberg et al., 2008; Shepard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: SAM levels may drop in MEFs upon CFIm knockdown.
source: Our work suggests that SAM levels may drop in MEFs upon CFIm knockdown, so it is possible that this SAM reduction contributes to the increased dedifferentiation potential, priming cells for transition into iPSC (Shiraki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings of this study.

claim: Cancer cells often have reduced methylation potential and/or intracellular SAM levels.
source: Similarly, it is plausible that SAM levels contribute to the growth potential of cancer cells, as cancer cells often have reduced methylation potential and/or intracellular SAM levels (Gao et al., 2019; Murray et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: CFIm knockdown may augment cancer growth by reducing SAM levels in addition to the well-defined 3´UTR shortening mechanism.
source: Therefore, CFIm knockdown may augment cancer growth by reducing SAM levels in addition to the well-defined 3´UTR shortening mechanism (Jafari Najaf Abadi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings of this study.
